summary: God’s absolute moral purity and otherness, the foundational attribute that makes sin a problem and grace a wonder
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 6:1-7 again, then turn to 1 Peter 1:14-16. Today is a doctrinal pause, so you are reading two passages together: Isaiah’s vision of the Holy One and Peter’s command that God’s people be holy. Ask as you read: what is holiness, and what does it have to do with me?
settingTheScene: Isaiah saw the Lord on a throne in the temple, and the seraphim cried, “Holy, holy, holy.” Seven centuries later, the apostle Peter wrote to scattered believers who were living as strangers in a pagan world, and he took a command from Leviticus: “You shall be holy, for I am holy.” Between them stands the central idea of the whole Bible. This is a day to stop and think carefully about what it means to say God is holy.
observation: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!” (Isaiah 6:3).
The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice, and the house was filled with smoke (Isaiah 6:4).
“Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5).
“Your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for” (Isaiah 6:7).
“As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance” (1 Peter 1:14).
“But as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct” (1 Peter 1:15).
“Since it is written, You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16).
The holiness commanded is rooted in the holiness of the one who calls.
doctrinalFocus:
To say that God is holy is to say first that he is different. The Hebrew word means “set apart” or “cut off.” God is not part of creation. He is not a bigger version of us. He is the Creator, infinitely above everything he has made, in power, in knowledge, in being. When the seraphim cover their faces and feet, they show that even the highest created beings cannot look at him without reverence.

Holiness also means that God is morally pure. In him there is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). He cannot tolerate evil, and he cannot be tempted by it. This is why Isaiah’s response to the vision was not delight but terror. In the presence of perfect purity, his own uncleanness was exposed. Holiness is not a cold attribute alone. It is bound up with God’s love, justice, and mercy. His love is a holy love, and his justice is a holy justice. This is why forgiveness is costly: a holy God cannot simply look away from sin. He deals with it, and he does so by providing atonement. The coal on the altar points to a sacrifice.

Third, holiness is shared. God does not remain in splendid isolation. He calls his people to be holy, as Peter says, in all their conduct. This is what it means to be saved: to be set apart for God, and to be changed to be like him. We are not holy by our own effort. In Christ, believers are already declared holy (1 Corinthians 1:2), and yet we are called to become holy in practice. Holiness is a gift we receive and a goal we pursue by the Spirit.

The right response to a holy God is reverence, repentance, and worship. And the good news is that the holy God has made a way to come near.
interpretation:
Put the two passages side by side and they teach a unified lesson. Isaiah’s vision shows us the God who is holy. Peter’s command shows us what holiness means for those who belong to him. Neither is possible without the other.

Isaiah’s experience follows an order: vision, confession, cleansing, and service. He did not choose to confess. The sight of God’s holiness did that for him. And the cleansing was not earned. The seraph brought the coal from the altar, and the declaration was made: “Your guilt is taken away.” Holiness begins with God’s initiative.

Peter writes to Christians who were tempted to go back to their old way of life. He tells them not to be conformed to the passions of their former ignorance. They once lived without knowing God. Now they have been called by a holy God, and they are to be holy. The command is based on the character of the one who calls. He does not say, be holy because it is difficult and noble. He says, be holy because I am.

The surrounding verses explain the foundation. Holiness comes from knowing that we have been ransomed “with the precious blood of Christ.” The holiness that God requires is the holiness that he has paid for. We are not trying to become acceptable. We have been made acceptable, and we now live out what is true of us.

This changes how we think about the Christian life. It is not mainly a list of rules but a way of life that reflects the character of the God we have met. We look at him, and we begin to be changed into the same image.
connection: Hebrews 12:14 says, “Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.” Hebrews 10:10 says we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ. 2 Corinthians 3:18 says we are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. 1 Thessalonians 4:7 says God has called us to holiness. Revelation 4:8 shows the living creatures still crying “Holy, holy, holy” before the throne.
application:
Take five minutes to sit before God without asking for anything. Let the word “holy” fill your mind.

Choose one area of life where your conduct does not reflect the God who called you. Ask for the Spirit’s help to change.

Thank God that holiness is first something he gives, in Christ, and not something you must earn.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for his holiness, and tell him how it moves you.
Thank him for taking away your guilt through Christ.
Ask him to make you holy as he is holy.
